Build a daily training-load series

Source: R/daily-load.R
as_daily_load.Rd

Converts a data frame with one row per training session (or per day) into a complete daily calendar with one row per athlete and day. This is the single entry point for every analysis in the package: descriptors and impulse-response models take a daily_load object.

Usage

as_daily_load(
  data,
  date,
  load,
  athlete = NULL,
  performance = NULL,
  gaps = c("rest", "missing"),
  max_gap = 7,
  date_format = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame with one row per session (or per day).

date

Name of the date column. The column must be of class Date, or character to be parsed with date_format. A Date with a fraction of a day is floored to the day. Date-times (POSIXct) are rejected: convert them with as.Date() first, choosing the time zone.

load

Name of the load column: numeric, >= 0 or NA. A column that is entirely NA (an empty column in a CSV file, read as logical) is accepted as numeric NA.

athlete

Name of the athlete identifier column, or NULL (the default) for a single athlete, who is labelled "1".

performance

Name of a numeric performance column, or NULL. At most one distinct non-NA value is allowed per athlete and day. An entirely NA column is accepted, as for load.

gaps

How to treat days with no row between an athlete's first and last date: "rest" (load 0, the default) or "missing" (load NA).

max_gap

A single non-negative whole number. A warning is given for each run of more than max_gap consecutive days without a row.

date_format

Format used to parse a character date column, as in strptime(). The default NULL accepts ISO dates ("%Y-%m-%d") only. Any parsed year before 1900 or after 2100 is an error, which catches two-digit years read with "%Y".

Value

An object of class c("daily_load", "data.frame") with one row per athlete and day, sorted by athlete and date, and the columns:

  • athlete (character);

  • date (Date), consecutive within each athlete;

  • load (numeric), the sum of the day's sessions;

  • status (factor with levels "training", "rest", "missing");

  • n_sessions (integer), the number of rows in data for that day, 0 for filled days;

  • filled (logical), TRUE for days that had no row;

  • performance (numeric), only if performance was given.

The attributes gaps and load_name record the gap option used and the name of the load column.

Day states

Every day has exactly one of three states (DECISIONS.md, D-015):

  • training: the load of the day is greater than 0;

  • rest: the load of the day is 0;

  • missing: the load of the day is not available (NA).

Sessions on the same day are summed. If any session of a day has an NA load, the whole day is NA and its state is "missing": a missing load is never silently replaced (D-016).

Gap rule

Each athlete's calendar runs from their own first to their own last date. Days in between that have no row are added and marked filled = TRUE. By default (gaps = "rest") they are treated as rest days with load 0; with gaps = "missing" they get load NA and state "missing" (D-015). The calendar ends at the athlete's last row: rest days after the last session are not added, so trailing rest days must be given as rows with load 0 to be included. A message reports how many days were filled. Whatever gaps is, a warning is given for every run of more than max_gap consecutive filled days, because a long run without data is as likely to be missing data as rest.

Several athletes and load columns

A data file may hold several athletes (identified by the column named in athlete) and several load columns; each call uses one load column (D-017). Its name is kept in the attribute load_name.

See also

print.daily_load(), summary.daily_load().

Examples

sessions <- data.frame(
  athlete = c("A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B"),
  date = c("2026-01-01", "2026-01-01", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-05",
           "2026-01-03", "2026-01-04"),
  srpe = c(300, 150, 0, NA, 420, 380),
  jump = c(41.2, NA, NA, 40.5, NA, 38.9)
)

x <- as_daily_load(sessions, date = "date", load = "srpe",
                   athlete = "athlete", performance = "jump")
#> Filled 2 days without a row as rest (load 0). Use gaps = "missing" to treat filled days as missing.
x
#> <daily_load> 2 athletes, 2026-01-01 to 2026-01-05, 7 days
#> Days: 3 training, 3 rest, 1 missing; 2 filled (as rest)
#> Load column: srpe
#> 
#>   athlete       date load   status n_sessions filled performance
#> 1       A 2026-01-01  450 training          2  FALSE        41.2
#> 2       A 2026-01-02    0     rest          1  FALSE          NA
#> 3       A 2026-01-03    0     rest          0   TRUE          NA
#> 4       A 2026-01-04    0     rest          0   TRUE          NA
#> 5       A 2026-01-05   NA  missing          1  FALSE        40.5
#> 6       B 2026-01-03  420 training          1  FALSE          NA
#> 7       B 2026-01-04  380 training          1  FALSE        38.9
summary(x)
#>   athlete first_date  last_date n_days n_training n_rest n_missing n_filled
#> 1       A 2026-01-01 2026-01-05      5          1      3         1        2
#> 2       B 2026-01-03 2026-01-04      2          2      0         0        0
#>   longest_filled_run n_performance
#> 1                  2             2
#> 2                  0             1

# Days without a row treated as missing instead of rest
as_daily_load(sessions, date = "date", load = "srpe",
              athlete = "athlete", gaps = "missing")
#> Filled 2 days without a row as missing (load NA).
#> <daily_load> 2 athletes, 2026-01-01 to 2026-01-05, 7 days
#> Days: 3 training, 1 rest, 3 missing; 2 filled (as missing)
#> Load column: srpe
#> 
#>   athlete       date load   status n_sessions filled
#> 1       A 2026-01-01  450 training          2  FALSE
#> 2       A 2026-01-02    0     rest          1  FALSE
#> 3       A 2026-01-03   NA  missing          0   TRUE
#> 4       A 2026-01-04   NA  missing          0   TRUE
#> 5       A 2026-01-05   NA  missing          1  FALSE
#> 6       B 2026-01-03  420 training          1  FALSE
#> 7       B 2026-01-04  380 training          1  FALSE
